A more than elementary grasp of mathematics (particularly statistics, which involves at least algebra and calculus) helps us see through the damn lies behind the numbers you read in the press.

For example, this came up yesterday. Without the jargon, the headline basically says "Thousands have died soon after having their benefit payments stopped". The headline is manipulative: it's designed to evoke an emotional reaction of "OMG, the government is basically killing people", but someone with more than basic numeracy would think: people die all the time, is the rate of these people dying more or less than the general rate of people dying? The numbers would tell you whether this was a significant amount of dying.

Furthermore, the sleazy government man said: "The mortality rate for people who have died while claiming an out-of-work benefit has fallen over a 10-year period. This is in line with the mortality rate for the general working-age population." Which may sound like everything's fine, but mathematics is more than numbers... you have to analyze what he's saying:

  1. The general death rate has dropped over 10 years.

  2. The death rate of people on benefits has dropped over 10 years.

But what he doesn't say is whether these rates are comparable. For example his statement could hold true in rather shocking circumstance. For example, say, 10 in 100,000 normal people died per year in 2005, and this dropped to 5 in 2015, while benefit claimants died at a rate of 1,000 in 100,000 in 2005 and 999 in 100,000 in 2015. So essentially, he's not saying anything meaningful at all, but it sounds reassuring.

TL; DR: To see through their smoke and mirror requires more than simple counting.

Luddite Horses

Imagine a pair of horses in the early 1900s talking about technology. One worries all these new mechanical muscles will make horses unnecessary.

The other reminds him that everything so far has made their lives easier -- remember all that farm work? Remember running coast-to-coast delivering mail? Remember riding into battle? All terrible. These city jobs are pretty cushy -- and with so many humans in the cities there are more jobs for horses than ever.

Even if this car thingy takes off you might say, there will be new jobs for horses we can't imagine.

But you, dear viewer, from beyond 2000 know what happened -- there are still working horses, but nothing like before. The horse population peaked in 1915 -- from that point on it was nothing but down.

There isn’t a rule of economics that says better technology makes more, better jobs for horses. It sounds shockingly dumb to even say that out loud, but swap horses for humans and suddenly people think it sounds about right.

As mechanical muscles pushed horses out of the economy, mechanical minds will do the same to humans. Not immediately, not everywhere, but in large enough numbers and soon enough that it's going to be a huge problem if we are not prepared. And we are not prepared.

You, like the second horse, may look at the state of technology now and think it can’t possibly replace your job. But technology gets better, cheaper, and faster at a rate biology can’t match.

I've been programming for over 30 years now, and i've done C, C++, PHP, Perl, Basic, Javascript, Prolog, Pascal, LOGO, Forth, VHDL, ML, lpc, SQL with a small amount of x86 Assembly, Objective C, Java, Ruby, Lua and Go.

Old style BASIC is a good language for introducing people to block structure languages such as the old style Cobol and Fortran. It usually provides all of the basic flow control structures, and this is very good for fundamentals if taught correctly. That is about it.

Using globals and gotos are somewhat detrimental, as globals impair performance even when you only have a few. Gotos don't have a way of keeping track of where you're coming from, so they force you to add more control structures to return correctly, which is why the Gosub came into being in the first place. Gotos are only really useful in one way jumps like switch statements or exception handling.

Modern things like functions and classes however do not exist, and to be honest you could learn these in a second or even third language without much difficulty, which is really imho, a better way to do things.

Introducing people to OOP too early screws over a lot of programmers ability and they don't even know it. I swear for every 20 people I interview that are primarily OOP programmers, only 1 has any good OOP programming skills and problem solving, and these often end up being people who started learning before the current fad of OOP programming. I end up having to retrain them so they can think outside of the OOP box. Its annoying. The last 20 years or so worth of programmers have been going down hill, sorry.

That said, I think you're okay if you let them learn something at least as complex as pascal to start. Python is a bit too strict, bash is a bit too quirky, javascript has scoping issues. PHP is a bit slow, but its decent as a second language because you can come from many different language backgrounds and use it effectively. I'm going to be mean a bit here, but Java is a horrible language. Java programmers much take longer than C++ programmers to do the same thing and then the result is slower. Somehow they have been convinced that Java can actually run faster than C (it can't, Sun's JVM is written mostly in C itself) Yes, you can get a lot out of Java's frameworks, and I'll give you that, but I can get PHP programmer to do the same thing in half the time and often it even runs faster.
